title: Sacks splitting

based_on.title: Lecture notes in Computability Theory
based_on.pages: December 3, 2008 version; section 31, Theorem 31.1 and Proposition 31.2, pp.62–67; Corollaries31.3,31.5–31.6; idle stages, least successful allowances, and the ordinary expansion decoder expanded

summary: Split any enumerable set into two low enumerable pieces, keeping a prescribed noncomputable limit-computable set beyond both pieces.
abstract: Friedberg splitting distributes the members of any undecidable enumerable set between two undecidable pieces. Sacks splitting gives finer control: both pieces can have jumps equivalent to ordinary halting, while neither computes a prescribed noncomputable set whose membership has convergent computable guesses. We protect successful oracle computations and increasing finite stretches of agreement with those guesses. If a piece computed the prescribed set, the protected stretches would supply an ordinary decision procedure for it, a contradiction. The same restraints eventually stop growing and yield convergent guesses for both jumps. Taking the prescribed set to be the input produces incomparable low pieces strictly below every nonzero enumerable degree. Their join still recovers the input, so two low sets can together have a nonlow join.
